title: How 4 YOE interviews work + roadmap
exp: Interviewers at ~4 years expect ownership of a vertical slice, production debugging, and clear trade-offs — not Staff-level CLR trivia. Typical loop: screen → technical (C#/ASP.NET/SQL) → small system design → behavioral/resume.
pts: **Junior vs 4 YOE vs Staff:** juniors show syntax; mid shows patterns + edge cases + tests; staff shapes org-wide architecture.
Product companies push design + debugging; consultancies push broad SOLID/SQL/Azure coverage.
Prepare **5 STAR stories**: incident, performance win, disagreement, mentoring, deadline trade-off.
Every resume bullet needs: your role, architecture sketch, hardest bug, metric, what you'd redo.
Prep cadence: 2–3 weeks focused on Parts in this path, then mock interviews.
pr: List every resume project with architecture + hardest bug

r: Deep dive into Day 1 runtime execution mechanics and threading constraints.
Focus on zero-allocation and lock-free patterns where applicable.
High concurrency contention or unexpected resource exhaustion under load.
Implement resilient backpressure, retries, and circuit breakers.
Balancing low latency, developer ergonomics, and system consistency.
Always state operational cost and complexity trade-offs.

qa.q: What do interviewers expect at ~4 YOE that they don't expect from a junior?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Trade-off reasoning, production debugging stories with metrics, ownership of API+DB+auth+observability end-to-end, and mentoring/communication — not just CRUD syntax.

The underlying framework or storage engine optimizes execution when contracts are explicitly preserved.

qa.q: How would you structure 2 weeks of prep before a mid-senior .NET interview?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Week 1: async, DI, ASP.NET pipeline, EF/SQL (N+1, indexes, isolation). Week 2: security, messaging, caching, observability, three system designs, and STAR/resume drills. Daily: 30–45 min flashcards + one design sketch.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Async methods compile into an IAsyncStateMachine struct managed by the AsyncMethodBuilder. Awaiting an uncompleted task yields execution back to the caller. Blocking with .Result on a thread bound to a SynchronizationContext causes deadlocks when the continuation waits for the blocked thread.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Sync-over-async (.Result or .Wait()) on ASP.NET request threads rapidly exhausts thread pool threads, leading to HTTP 503 gateway timeouts and request queuing under load.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Async all the way preserves thread pool scalability, but requires passing CancellationToken through all layers and avoiding sync blocking methods everywhere.
